confirmed_blank.note: Confirmed blank across the bank's own reports and its supreme audit institution. Read: Banque Centrale de Djibouti Rapport Annuel 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 (banque-centrale.dj), governance chapter 'Comite d'audit / Audit interne / Controle interne' in each. Those sections say the Audit Committee held two meetings a year, that the business put to those meetings was 'epuiser les reflexions internes engagees sur le projet relatif au code de deontologie' (a code of ethics still in draft) and the implementation of recommendations, that the Internal Audit Charter was adopted by the Board on 24 December 2018, and that 'le dispositif de controle de la Banque est appele a etre renforce'. No staff case, no discipline, no fraud, no irregularity is named in any of the eight years. The external auditor changed from Ernst & Young to Deloitte from 2021. Also read the bank's own external audit report: 'BCD Rapport d'audit sur les etats financiers annuels, exercice clos le 31 decembre 2020', Ernst & Young S.A., signed Abidjan 10 February 2022 - a clean unqualified opinion, no emphasis-of-matter and no key-audit-matter paragraph; the only mentions of 'fraude' are the standard ISA responsibility wording. Second source type also read: Djibouti's Chambre des Comptes et de Discipline Budgetaire, Rapport Public General Annuel 2021 Tome 1 (hosted at aisccuf.org), both halves of the 158,496-character document. The Banque Centrale de Djibouti is not mentioned anywhere in it. The entities examined are the Hopital General Peltier and the Agence Djiboutienne des Routes, plus thematic chapters on the public-procurement code and the anti-corruption bodies (CNMP, IGE, IGF, CNPLC, SRF); its findings are against the hospital and the roads agency (a 9,450,000 FDJ purchase split in two to stay under the 5,000,000 FDJ tender threshold; 394,390,050 FDJ of payments without supporting documents at ADR), not the central bank.

Confirmed blank, and the bank publishes the figures that make it checkable. Read: Danmarks Nationalbank Aarsrapport 2018, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 (nationalbanken.dk), the 'Whistleblowerordning' section of the management report in each, plus the whole audit report in each. 2025, in the bank's own words: 'Der er i 2025 modtaget to indberetninger, som begge er afvist af det eksterne advokatfirma, da de ikke vedrorte Nationalbanken' - two reports, both rejected by the external law firm because they did not concern the Nationalbank. 2024: nine reports, of which four were supplements to reports received in 2023 and one was a follow-up to a report made in 2017; the report says none of them gave rise to further investigation under the scheme, all 2024 reports were anonymous to management, and the assessment was that they involved no serious matters concerning current employees or the bank's activities. The scheme is run by an external law firm, not by the bank. Also read: the bank's standing whistleblower page (nationalbanken.dk/en/legal-information/whistleblower-scheme), which tabulates 2021 and 2022 at zero reports, 2023 at 1 received and 1 rejected, 2024 at 9 received and 9 rejected, 2025 at 2 received and 2 rejected, with the 'Reports investigated' and 'Reports resulting in a police report' columns marked N/A for every year. The audit reports' many mentions of 'besvigelser' (fraud) are the standard auditor-responsibility wording from PricewaterhouseCoopers, not findings.

Confirmed blank across the bank's own reports and the parliamentary review of them. Read: Reserve Bank of Fiji Annual Report 2012, 2018, August 2022-July 2023 and August 2023-July 2024, the 'Staffing' / 'Human Resources' and 'Governance' sections of each. The governance sections say the Board Governance Committee approves a Fraud Prevention policy, a Whistleblower policy and a Code of Conduct, that staff complete quarterly Fraud Declarations and conflict-of-interest declarations, and that staff are trained on whistleblowing. Not one declaration, case or breach is reported as having been made. The 2012 report's staffing paragraph records that nine staff resigned, 'one staff was dismissed and two long serving staff retired from service' - it gives no reason for the dismissal and does not connect it to misconduct, so it is not a case. Second source type also read: Fiji Parliament, Standing Committee on Economic Affairs, 'Consolidated Review Report of the Reserve Bank of Fiji 2018-2021 Annual Reports' (April 2022) and the 'Appendices' volume to the consolidated review of the 2021-2024 annual reports (August 2025, containing the RBF's written submission and the committee's questions). Neither contains any mention of discipline, misconduct, fraud, irregularity, investigation, termination or breach at the bank. Checked and excluded: FICAC's own press releases that surface on this search are about the Fiji Development Bank, a state development bank, not the central bank - its former Relationship and Sales Officer Joji Cavalevu was charged in 2023 over about $36,000 of falsified receipts and found to have a case to answer on 19 charges in 2026.

Confirmed blank for the document read, and both of the bank's own publishing hosts are unreadable from here. The inversion test that closed Saudi Arabia also closes the audit-institution route for Oman: Oman Daily's full account of the State Audit Institution's annual report ('jihaz al-riqaba': recovery of 177.7 million rials for the public treasury, omandaily.om article 1165826) lists every body the Institution examined that year - the Ministry of Education's schools, Sultan Qaboos University's operating contracts, the University of Technology and Applied Sciences, the Agricultural and Fisheries Development Fund, the Oman Investment Authority, Dhofar Municipality's building project, the governors' offices, Petroleum Development Oman's service contracts, OQ Methanol, Oman LNG, Dhofar Integrated Services and Oman Sewerage Services. The Central Bank of Oman is not among them. The 28 cases the Institution says it referred to the Public Prosecution are not attributed to any named body, so that line cannot be keyed to the central bank. Separately, the one Omani embezzlement conviction that surfaces in Arabic - about 6 million rials recovered, defendants convicted (omandaily.om article 1121826) - is Oman Arab Bank, a commercial bank, not the central bank. The annual-report vein itself is UNREAD for Oman: see needs_a_hand_check.

Annual-report vein now tested, which the existing gaps note said had not been. Read: Brunei Darussalam Central Bank Annual Report 2022 and Annual Report 2023 (cms.bdcb.gov.bn), the Audit Committee passage in the governance chapter, the 'Internal Audit' passage and the 'Integrity' passage in the Organisational Development chapter, and the whole audit report. The 2023 Internal Audit passage names the year's actual audit work: a consultancy review on the Business Sentiment Index process, a process review on Legal Affairs, facilitation of the retest verification for the second SWIFT Customer Security Programme independent assessment on the payment and settlement system, and completion of an internal audit system migration. No finding against any person or unit. The 2023 'Integrity' passage describes bite-sized reminders of existing policies circulated to employees under the name 'HR Shares' and four engagement sessions on standards of conduct and ethics, one of them run by the Royal Brunei Police Force's Women and Children Abuse Investigation Unit on harassment and bullying in the workplace - awareness training, not cases. Every other hit on fraud in both reports is BDCB as the regulator: the Notice on Reporting of Fraud Incidents for Banks, Finance Companies and Insurance Companies/Takaful Operators, which requires the institutions it supervises to report fraud incidents to the bank. The bank is the recipient of those reports, not the subject.

needs_a_hand_check.note: OFFERED AND, I think, REFUSED BY THE SETTLED RULE - recorded so the next round does not spend itself here. Bo Bo Nge, deputy governor of the Central Bank of Myanmar, was arrested on 1 February 2021, the day of the coup, and removed from his post. More than a year later the military council's anti-corruption commission charged him under section 55 of the Anti-Corruption Law, a charge carrying 15 years, in a case filed at Phayagon central police station in Naypyitaw's Ottarathiri Township; he was sentenced to 20 years in December 2022. The alleged conduct is central-bank conduct on its face: that he failed to tax a withdrawal on 8 February 2021 of about US$1.4m in kyat out of US$5m that Open Society Myanmar had deposited in 2018 at the Small and Medium Enterprise Development Bank, costing the state 360m kyat (about US$200,000); that he did not take the best available interest rates when central bank funds were placed with private institutions; and that he did not enforce reporting of foreign transactions above US$10,000. But the withdrawal he is said to have failed to tax happened on 8 February 2021, a week after he was arrested and removed, so he was in military custody when it occurred. That makes this a prosecution of a removed official by the body that removed him - the category the map refused for Sudan in rounds 52 and 66 - and not a corruption case. Source: Myanmar Now, 'Detained deputy governor of Myanmar's central bank hit with major corruption charge', https://www.myanmar-now.org/en/news/detained-deputy-governor-of-myanmars-central-bank-hit-with-major-corruption-charge . My recommendation is to add MMR to cases_unavailable with this reasoning rather than to carry it as a record.

A judgment call for the owner, not a record I am willing to file on my own. The only thing in Danish reach that is a report of possible wrongdoing at the bank is the bank's own whistleblower tally. Danmarks Nationalbank Aarsrapport 2024 states that nine reports were received under the scheme in 2024, that four of them were supplements to reports received in 2023 and one was a follow-up to a report made in 2017, that none of them led to further investigation under the scheme, and that the assessment was that there were no serious matters concerning current employees or the bank's activities. If the map wants to carry 'allegation, no outcome reported' entries then this is one, with a status line of 'reports received 2017, 2023 and 2024; none investigated under the scheme; bank states no serious matter found'. If it only carries findings, this is a blank and belongs where I have put it in confirmed_blank. I have not written it as a record because the source reports the reports being declined, not any finding, and filing it would read as a Danish corruption case when the document says the opposite. Source: https://nationalbanken.dk/media/rsdd5dyu/aarsrapport-2024.pdf (Whistleblowerordning section) and https://www.nationalbanken.dk/en/legal-information/whistleblower-scheme .

A real thread, left hanging by one missing section. The Central Bank of Sudan's 64th Annual Report 2024 (Arabic, cbos.gov.sd) prints, at page 50, the audit opinion of the National Audit Chamber signed by Mohamed Elhafiz Mohamed Nasr FCCA, Deputy Auditor General for Bodies and Companies, dated 2 September 2025. It is a QUALIFIED opinion: 'fi ra'yina, bistithna' al-ta'thirat al-muhtamala lil-amr al-muwaddah fi qism asas al-ra'y fi taqrirna' - in our opinion, except for the possible effects of the matter described in the Basis for Opinion section of our report. The Basis for Opinion section itself is NOT printed in the annual report; the opinion paragraph refers to a section the published document omits. So the National Audit Chamber has qualified the central bank's 2024 accounts over a named matter and the matter is not in the bank's own publication. What would settle it is the National Audit Chamber's own report on the bank, or the full auditor's report. Read and clean otherwise: the chapter 'Hisabat Bank al-Sudan al-Markazi lil-'am 2024' and the whole 2024 Arabic report, in which fasad, ikhtilas, rashwa, mukhalafat, ta'dib, tajawuzat and nazaha do not occur at all; and the English Annual Reports 2013, 2014 and 2016, whose only hits on fraud, discipline, irregularity and governance are macro-policy phrasing ('disciplined fiscal policies') and the bank's corporate-governance rules for the commercial banks it supervises.

The annual-report vein is untested for Oman because both hosts refuse to serve the file, not because the file is clean. The Central Bank of Oman's publications page (https://cbo.gov.om/Pages/AnnualReport.aspx) offers exactly three annual reports, 2023, 2024 and 2025, all at https://publishing.bnet.om/sites/assets/Documents/English/Publications/AnnualReports/Annual%20Report%20<year>%20ENG.pdf . The gateway answers 502 to CONNECT for publishing.bnet.om (host allowed, gateway cannot reach it) and the page fetcher is refused by that host's robots.txt. cbo.gov.om itself serves an incomplete TLS chain and curl cannot verify it; the page fetcher can read cbo.gov.om HTML but not the PDFs. web.archive.org's CDX endpoint resets the connection from here, so no archived copy could be enumerated either. Anyone who can reach publishing.bnet.om should grep those three reports for the internal-audit, governance and staff sections.

Also untested rather than clean, for a different reason. The Banco de Cabo Verde publishes its Relatorio e Contas through a SharePoint list at https://www.bcv.cv/pt/Estatisticas/Publicacoes%20e%20Intervencoes/Relatorios/Paginas/Relatorios.aspx . The page is 816,703 bytes of markup and exposes no PDF URL at all - the list is rendered by script - and the SharePoint document-library and REST paths answer 404 and 403. Search engines do not index any bcv.cv annual report PDF; every Cabo Verde 'Relatorio e Contas' that surfaces belongs to a commercial bank (Caixa Economica, BCN, BCA). The site's own homepage link to the reports page was the only route found. A browser that runs the page's script, or the Boletim Oficial (boe.incv.cv), would get at these.

One finding exists that touches the Bank of Eritrea, and it is not a corruption case against the bank. UN Security Council, Report of the Monitoring Group on Somalia and Eritrea, S/2013/440, footnote 119, describes Eritrea running two parallel economies and says hard currency deposits are 'officially managed by a hard currency oversight board, comprising representatives of the Ministry of National Development, the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Eritrea, the Commercial Bank of Eritrea and the Director of the PFDJ Economic Affairs Department, Hagos Gebrehiwot', and then: 'While the Bank of Eritrea may, in theory, exist as the country's apex hard currency depository, in practice, hard currency appropriation takes place through a number of banks and informal channels.' That is a finding about the state's financial architecture, with the bank named as one seat on a board; it names no official of the bank and alleges no act by the bank, so I have not written it as a record. Source: https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/atf/cf/%7B65BFCF9B-6D27-4E9C-8CD3-CF6E4FF96FF9%7D/s_2013_440.pdf . The companion reports S/2011/652, S/2012/545, S/2014/727 and S/2015/802 could not be opened: digitallibrary.un.org answers HTTP 202 to every request from here and serves no file, and docs.un.org and undocs.org return 4KB stubs. S/2011/433, which S/2013/440 cites as the origin of the parallel-economy finding, is unread for the same reason. Himbol Financial Services, the Eritrean remittance arm these reports discuss, should be checked for whether any report states it is an arm of the Bank of Eritrea rather than of the PFDJ - that is the one thing that would turn this into a central-bank record.

searched_no_result.note: The Bank of Eritrea publishes nothing: no annual report, no financial statements, no governance or audit section, in any language, on any host that search returns. There is no primary document to grep, so the annual-report method cannot be run on Eritrea at all. Eritrea has no published supreme audit institution report either.

The Central Bank of Myanmar's annual reports could not be located. cbm.gov.mm returns 404 for /content/annual-report and its homepage exposes only opaque numeric /content/<id> links with no report titles; search returns no cbm.gov.mm annual report PDF for any year. The only CBM periodical that surfaces on a reachable host is a half-year transaction report for fiscal 2018, mirrored by the France-Myanmar chamber of commerce. Checked and excluded: 'Myanmar Central Bank takes stern action on 20 people for illegal money transfers' (January 2024) is the bank acting against outside money changers, so the bank is the enforcer and not the subject - the same inversion that disqualified the Saudi Nazaha statements.

leads_not_opened.note: From the existing gaps note rather than my own work, but it is the cheapest unopened lead on the whole list: the Auditor-General's Office of Singapore audits the Monetary Authority of Singapore every year because the MAS Act names no other auditor, which makes each AGO annual report from FY2012/13 to FY2024/25 a separate checkable document. Only FY2023/24 has been read.

Danmarks Nationalbank's Aarsrapport exists back to at least 2004 on nationalbanken.dk, but the whistleblower section only begins with the 2021 scheme. The pre-2021 years would have to be checked through the Folketing's Finance Committee instead; two committee annexes about the Nationalbank sit on ft.dk (samling/20121/almdel/FIU/bilag/117 and samling/20111/almdel/FIU/bilag/143) and were not opened.

Fiji's Office of the Auditor-General annual reports were not opened. The RBF's own statements are audited by its external auditor, so whether the OAG examines the bank at all is unknown; if it does, those reports are the Singapore-style inversion test for Fiji. Parliament's site hosts them.

Sudan's National Audit Chamber (Diwan al-Muraja'a al-Qawmi) has no reachable site in any search result from here, so its own report on the central bank - which holds the Basis for Opinion paragraph the bank's annual report leaves out - is unopened. The bank's own Arabic annual reports for 2012 and 2021, and the 58th report for 2018, exist only on cbos01jo2022.dev2.dot.jo, a development host for the bank's site; I did not read them there.
